title: Members and encapsulation map
intro: This module teaches how to define your own types in C# — classes, structs, fields, properties, methods, constructors, and access modifiers. You will learn how the Common Language Runtime (CLR) enforces encapsulation, when to pick a class versus a struct, and how C# 14 features like the `field` keyword and partial constructors fit in.

overviewDiagram.title: Building a type step by step
overviewDiagram.source:
flowchart TD
  START[Choose type kind] --> CLASS[class — reference, identity]
  START --> STRUCT[struct — value, copy]
  CLASS --> MEMBERS[Add members]
  STRUCT --> MEMBERS
  MEMBERS --> FIELDS[Fields — private storage]
  MEMBERS --> PROPS[Properties — public accessors]
  MEMBERS --> METHODS[Methods — behavior]
  MEMBERS --> CTOR[Constructors — creation]
  METHODS --> PARAMS[Ordinary parameters first]
  PARAMS --> REF[ref / in / out — aliasing]
  MEMBERS --> ACCESS[Access modifiers — visibility]
  MEMBERS --> STATIC[Static members — type-level]
  MEMBERS --> EXTRA[Enums, tuples, indexers]
  MEMBERS --> PARTIAL[Partial types — multi-file]
  MEMBERS --> OPS[Operator overloading — last]

conceptCards.title: Classes and instances
conceptCards.summary: A class is a reference-type blueprint. `new` creates a heap object; variables hold references, not copies.
conceptCards.example: var b = a; // both point at the same object

conceptCards.title: Fields and properties
conceptCards.summary: Fields store data privately. Properties are the versionable public surface with get, set, and init accessors.

conceptCards.title: Methods and parameters
conceptCards.summary: Methods are named operations. Ordinary parameters copy values or references. Overloads differ by parameter types.

conceptCards.title: ref, in, and out
conceptCards.summary: ref aliases a variable both ways. in is a readonly alias. out must be assigned by the callee.
conceptCards.example: bool TryParse(string s, out int result)

conceptCards.title: Constructors and required
conceptCards.summary: Constructors initialize objects. Primary constructors capture inputs. required forces object initializers to be complete.
conceptCards.example: public class Cmd(string exchange) { public required string Key { get; init; } }

conceptCards.title: Access modifiers
conceptCards.summary: public, private, protected, internal, protected internal, private protected, and file. CLR enforces them at runtime.
conceptCards.example: Members default to private; types default to internal.

conceptCards.title: Static members
conceptCards.summary: Static belongs to the type, not instances. One shared copy per type load. Great for utilities, dangerous for mutable state.
conceptCards.example: public static class Math { public static int Max(int a, int b) => a > b ? a : b; }

conceptCards.title: Structs versus classes
conceptCards.summary: Structs copy on assignment. Classes alias. Use readonly struct for small immutable data; class for identity and lifetime.
conceptCards.example: readonly struct CacheKey(string tenant, string id)

conceptCards.title: Enums, tuples, and indexers
conceptCards.summary: Enums name integer constants. Tuples group values without a type declaration. Indexers provide collection-like access.

conceptCards.title: Partial types
conceptCards.summary: partial splits one type across files. Source generators declare; you implement. C# 14 adds partial constructors and events.
conceptCards.example: public partial class Worker { public partial Worker(string path); }

conceptCards.title: Operator overloading
conceptCards.summary: Operators are static methods with special syntax. Use on value-like types. C# 14 adds user-defined compound assignment.
conceptCards.example: public static Money operator +(Money a, Money b)
